title: Boy A
full_review:
"Boy A" (Weinstein) is the achingly sad and touching story of a sensitive young man (stunning work by Andrew Garfield), released from prison after 14 years for a dreadful crime in which he took part as a child.

With the help of Terry (Peter Mullan), his concerned caseworker and surrogate father, he tries to start anew with the assumed name of Jack. (The disguise is necessary as the papers have dredged up the crime, and the public is still screaming for the blood of the young criminal known only as Boy A.)

Terry helps him land a job with a delivery company where he bonds with fellow employee Chris (Shaun Evans), who becomes his partner. With Chris' encouragement, Jack summons the nerve to ask office clerk Michelle (Katie Lyons) for a date, and she eventually falls for his shy, faltering ways. He's never had a relationship with a woman before, but the love he comes to feel for her is genuine and profound.

 

Throughout, there are flashbacks of Jack's unhappy childhood with a dying mother and distant father at home and cruel bullying at school. Eventually, he fell under the influence of an emotionally damaged -- and sometimes violent -- classmate who offered him the only friendship he had ever known.

 

We don't learn the details of the actual crime until the movie is nearly over. Meanwhile, we've empathized with this very likable young man, and even witnessed a spontaneous act of heroism on his part that will ironically have dreadful repercussions.

Director John Crowley's film is bleak, heart-wrenching, morally complex and thought-provoking with themes of forgiveness, redemption, the negative influence of the media, and the human tendency to form premature judgments.

 

Scriptwriter Mark O'Rowe's adaptation of John Trigell's novel shows compassion toward nearly all the characters, revealing the motivation behind even terrible deeds.

This could be a star-making vehicle for Garfield, but all the performances are finely judged.

 

The film contains rough language and profanity, crude expressions, nongraphic sexual situations and frank discussion, fleeting upper female nudity, bodily violence, an off-screen murder, suicide, and brief drug use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
